title: Missed Calls Are Costing You Customers. Here’s How to Fix It
description: Why missed calls quietly drain revenue for local businesses, how to measure the problem, and five practical ways to make sure every caller gets an answer.
body:
For many local businesses, the phone is still the most valuable sales channel. A caller is usually ready to buy, book or hire right now. When that call goes to voicemail, many people simply hang up and call the next business on the list.

Step one: measure the problem

Most owners underestimate how many calls they miss. Before fixing anything, find out:

  • How many calls go unanswered each week, from your phone system or carrier reports.
  • When they happen: after hours, lunch, weekends or busy mornings.
  • How many missed callers leave a voicemail, and how many never call back.

Multiply missed calls by your typical close rate and average customer value, and you have a rough monthly cost. Our missed-call calculator does this math for you.

Five ways to answer every call

1. Fix your hours and voicemail first

Make sure your Google Business Profile shows accurate hours and that your voicemail tells callers exactly what happens next and when they’ll hear back.

2. Call back fast

If you can’t answer, a quick callback matters. Set a team rule and a reminder for every missed call.

3. Add text-back

An automatic text to missed callers (“Sorry we missed you, how can we help?”) keeps the conversation alive and lets busy customers reply when it suits them.

4. Use an AI receptionist for overflow and after hours

An AI receptionist can answer instantly, handle common questions and book appointments into your calendar, then send your team a summary. Many businesses start with after-hours calls only.

5. Route urgent calls to a person

Whatever you use, define what counts as urgent and make sure those calls reach someone immediately.

Track the results

After a month, compare answered calls, booked appointments and new customers against your starting numbers. The goal isn’t technology for its own sake; it’s fewer customers slipping away.
